ideas.title: Cloud-computer errand agents
ideas.tagline: Tell one app a goal; it works in a cloud browser and pings your iPhone for logins and the Pay button.
ideas.moment: It is Sunday night and you have three errands: return a jacket, book a haircut, renew a parking permit. You dictate them into one app, lock the phone, and a Live Activity ticks through each one while the agent works in its own cloud browser. It stops twice: once for a password, once before paying.
ideas.problem: Small online errands each take ten minutes of logins, forms and hunting for the right page, and they pile up. Chat assistants can explain how to do them but not do them. An iPhone app cannot operate Safari or other apps, so any agent that clicks through websites has to run somewhere else and still needs you at the risky moments.

loop.trigger: You say or type a goal, or a schedule fires
loop.senses: Pages in its cloud browser, linked accounts
loop.decides: The next step, and whether it needs you
loop.checks_with_you: Logins, CAPTCHAs and every payment
loop.acts: Fills forms, sends email, books, checks out
loop.remembers: Your sizes, sites, preferences, past runs

ios_blocks.name: ActivityKit (Live Activities, push-to-start)
ios_blocks.why: shows each step of a cloud run on the Lock Screen, started by the server

ios_blocks.name: UserNotifications (UNNotificationAction)
ios_blocks.why: approval prompts with Approve and Decline buttons

ios_blocks.name: App Intents (App Shortcuts, SnippetIntent)
ios_blocks.why: start an errand from Siri or the Action button and confirm it in an interactive snippet

ios_blocks.name: AuthenticationServices (ASWebAuthenticationSession)
ios_blocks.why: OAuth into mail, calendar and store accounts without handing over passwords

ios_blocks.name: LocalAuthentication
ios_blocks.why: Face ID before a payment or a shared login

ios_blocks.name: CryptoKit (SecureEnclave)
ios_blocks.why: signs each approval so the server can prove it came from your phone

hard_parts: Long runs break. Sites change layouts, time out and throw CAPTCHAs; CNN's test of Muse saw a purchase stall at a store that required a professional licence.
Logins. Many sites block cloud-browser traffic or send 2FA codes by SMS, which a third-party iOS app cannot read, so the user has to relay codes or approve each sign-in by hand.
The phone cannot host the loop. Every state change has to come back by push, and a Live Activity lasts at most 8 hours, so multi-day errands fall back to plain notifications.
Cost. A long run on a frontier model in a cloud VM costs real money per task, while Meta, OpenAI and Google bundle the same thing into free or $20 plans.
risks: Prompt injection: a page or email the agent reads can tell it to send data or buy something. Confirmations must be drawn by the app from the real action, not written by the model.
One service holds sessions and cookies for many accounts, so one breach exposes all of them.
Many sites forbid automated access in their terms, and App Review guideline 5.2.2 expects apps to have permission to use the third-party services they act on.
assumptions: People will hand one company the logins to many services, as long as money and passwords still need their tap.
Websites keep tolerating agent traffic instead of blocking it or demanding agent-only APIs.
The cost of a 30-step run keeps falling fast enough to fit inside a consumer subscription.
unknowns: Who pays when the agent submits the wrong form or buys the wrong item?
Will Apple ever let a third-party agent act in Safari, the way its own Passwords agent changes passwords?
Does one general agent keep winning once each errand type has a specialist app?

prior_art.name: Meta Muse
prior_art.note: Email, travel, forms, checkout with one-time cards and business calls from Meta's cloud computer; US and 18+ only.

prior_art.name: ChatGPT agent and Work tab
prior_art.note: Cloud-browser tasks started by voice on iPhone since Sept 23, 2026; Work tab is for Plus and Pro.

prior_art.name: Gemini Spark
prior_art.note: 24/7 agent across Gmail, Docs and signed-in sites; loads checkout pages but hands payment back to you. Pro and Ultra only.

prior_art.name: Manus
prior_art.note: Virtual-computer agent whose iPhone app shows every step; bought by Meta in December 2025.

prior_art.name: Genspark Super Agent
prior_art.note: 80+ tools including Call for Me; strong on documents and research, less on logged-in errands.

ideas.first_version: Pick one errand family with stable web flows, such as returns and exchanges at the 50 biggest US retailers. Run it in a cloud browser, stream each step to a Live Activity, and stop for login and a Face ID approval before any submit. Keep a replayable screenshot log of every run.
ideas.notes_for_editor: Muse download and chart figures come from 9to5Mac and other press, not Apple. The CNN Muse test (https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/23/tech/meta-muse-ai-agent) is cited from the research notes; I did not open it. The Manus price (reported $2B+) is unconfirmed.

ideas.title: Phone-call errand agents
ideas.tagline: An agent phones businesses from a cloud number to get quotes, hold slots and wait on hold, then reports back.
ideas.moment: Your car needs brakes and you hate calling around. You give the agent the car, your zip code and a budget. Twenty minutes later you have three shop quotes and a Thursday slot on hold, and you never dialed.
ideas.problem: Many small businesses still give quotes and bookings only by phone. Calling around eats an afternoon of phone trees, hold music and repeating your details. iOS gives third-party apps no way to place or listen to cellular calls, and Apple's own Hold Assist only waits; it never talks.

loop.trigger: You ask for quotes, a booking or a fix
loop.senses: Business listings and the live call audio
loop.decides: Who to call, what to ask, what to accept
loop.checks_with_you: Before booking, paying or sharing IDs
loop.acts: Calls from a cloud number, works phone trees
loop.remembers: Quotes, reference numbers, who picked up

ios_blocks.name: MapKit (MKLocalSearch)
ios_blocks.why: finds nearby businesses and their phone numbers to build the call list

ios_blocks.name: ActivityKit (Live Activities)
ios_blocks.why: shows dialing, on hold and talking states on the Lock Screen

ios_blocks.name: UserNotifications
ios_blocks.why: delivers results and asks before the agent commits to anything

ios_blocks.name: App Intents
ios_blocks.why: start a call task from Siri or the Action button

ios_blocks.name: LiveCommunicationKit
ios_blocks.why: lets you join the cloud call over VoIP when the business insists on the customer

hard_parts: Calls have to come from cloud telephony (Genspark runs on Twilio), so caller ID shows an unknown number that busy shops ignore or that carriers may label as spam.
Handoff. When a clerk needs the customer, the agent has to bridge you in over VoIP within seconds or the call is lost.
Identity checks. Account PINs, last-four digits and 'are you the account holder?' stop the agent cold unless the user is patched in.
Recording and transcription rules differ by US state, and some states require every party to agree before a call is recorded.
risks: The agent must say it is an AI calling for a customer. Letting it pass as the customer invites fraud claims and angry businesses.
Accidental commitments: a 'hold' turns into a booking with a cancellation fee. Keep holding and booking as separate, approved steps.
Businesses may start blocking agent calls or answering with their own AI, turning calls into bot-to-bot loops.
assumptions: Businesses keep answering calls from AI agents instead of blocking them or putting their own AI receptionist on the line.
Real-time voice stays cheap enough to spend 30 minutes on hold for one task.
unknowns: Will carrier spam labeling start flagging agent calls at scale?
How often does a call end up needing the human after all, and do users pick up when patched in?
Will Apple ever open Hold Assist or call audio to third-party apps?

prior_art.name: Google 'Let Google Call'
prior_art.note: Calls local businesses about prices and availability from Search; grew out of the 'Ask for Me' Labs test. Information calls only.

prior_art.name: Genspark Call for Me
prior_art.note: Multilingual outbound calls for bookings and customer service, on Twilio Programmable Voice.

prior_art.name: Meta Muse calls
prior_art.note: Outbound calls to US businesses switched on around Sept 17, 2026, inside a general agent.

prior_art.name: Assindo
prior_art.note: Consumer call agent that waits on hold and works IVR menus on iOS, Android and web; claims are from its own site.

ideas.first_version: Quote calls only. The user names a service and an area; the agent calls up to five local shops from a cloud number with a fixed script and returns a comparison table. It never books; it only asks a shop to hold a slot for an hour, with a one-tap VoIP join if the shop wants the customer.
ideas.notes_for_editor: The Muse call launch date (about Sept 17, 2026) comes from 9to5Mac. Assindo's features are self-described. The Genspark and Twilio link comes from a Business Wire release listed in the research notes.

ideas.title: Inbox triage-and-draft agents
ideas.tagline: An agent sorts your mail, writes replies in your voice and leaves them in Drafts for you to send.
ideas.moment: You open your mail app at 7am and 14 replies are already drafted in your tone. You fix one sentence, send nine, and see that the agent filed the newsletters and flagged the one invoice that needs you.
ideas.problem: Email is a stream of small decisions: reply, file, pay or ignore. Most AI mail features summarize and leave the work to you. On iPhone, no app can read Mail.app (MailKit is macOS-only), so an inbox agent must connect to Gmail or Outlook servers directly or be your mail client.

loop.trigger: New mail lands in Gmail or Outlook
loop.senses: Threads, your sent mail, your calendar
loop.decides: Label, draft, flag, or leave alone
loop.checks_with_you: You send every draft yourself
loop.acts: Labels threads, saves replies to Drafts
loop.remembers: Your tone, VIPs, rules you corrected

ios_blocks.name: AuthenticationServices (ASWebAuthenticationSession)
ios_blocks.why: OAuth sign-in to Gmail or Microsoft Graph for the server-side agent

ios_blocks.name: UserNotifications
ios_blocks.why: pushes only the few threads that need you

ios_blocks.name: App Intents mail schema (AppSchema.MailIntent: createDraft, sendDraft)
ios_blocks.why: lets Siri AI act on drafts, but only if the app is itself the mail client

ios_blocks.name: WidgetKit
ios_blocks.why: a Home Screen count of drafts waiting and threads that need you

hard_parts: Gmail's read and draft scopes are restricted: Google requires app verification and a recurring third-party security assessment before a public app can read mail.
Sounding like you. Drafts need your sent mail as examples and a way to learn from your edits without mixing in anyone else's mail.
Prompt injection through mail. An incoming message can carry instructions; the EchoLeak flaw (CVE-2025-32711) showed one crafted email could make Microsoft 365 Copilot leak data.
No iOS mail hook. The agent runs on a server and writes into your mailbox; the phone only gets pushes and a review screen.
risks: A draft that promises something you never agreed to, sent in a hurry. Sending should stay a human tap by default.
Mail holds password resets and bank alerts, so a breach of the agent is an account-takeover risk.
App Review guideline 5.1.2(i) requires naming the AI provider and getting consent before mail content goes to a third-party model.
assumptions: Google and Microsoft keep granting broad read-and-draft API scopes to third-party agents.
People actually read drafts before sending instead of rubber-stamping them.
unknowns: Will Gmail's own AI Inbox make third-party triage redundant for most people?
What share of drafts get sent unedited, and does it hold after the first month?

prior_art.name: Superhuman Go
prior_art.note: Directs first-party and partner agents (Box, Gamma and others) and has an iOS app; built for heavy email users.

prior_art.name: Gmail AI Inbox
prior_art.note: Summaries, topics and to-dos inside Gmail; went to trusted testers first in January 2026.

prior_art.name: Fyxer
prior_art.note: Sorts and drafts inside Gmail and Outlook; no iPhone app, but its drafts show up in any mail app.

prior_art.name: Shortwave
prior_art.note: AI-native Gmail client with a multi-step assistant; web-first.

ideas.first_version: A server-side Gmail connector that sorts each new thread into four buckets and drafts replies only to people you have written to before. The iPhone app shows a morning stack of drafts to send, edit or discard with a swipe. The agent never sends anything itself.
ideas.notes_for_editor: Fyxer and Shortwave details come from review blogs, not the companies. I did not re-check the current terms of Google's restricted-scope security assessment (CASA); the wording is kept general on purpose.

ideas.title: Scheduling negotiator agents
ideas.tagline: CC or text an assistant; it trades times with the other side, sends the invite and chases replies.
ideas.moment: A client emails asking to meet next week. You reply-all, copy your scheduling assistant with 'find 30 minutes', and go back to your run. By lunch the invite is on both calendars with a video link and a note about the time zone.
ideas.problem: Finding a time takes three to six messages, and each one waits on somebody. Booking links push the work onto the other person, and some find them rude. AI calendars that rearrange your week mostly plan on a laptop, and their iPhone apps only view and edit.

loop.trigger: You CC or text the assistant on a thread
loop.senses: The thread, your calendar, your rules
loop.decides: Which times to offer, and in what order
loop.checks_with_you: Only when a request breaks your rules
loop.acts: Emails times, sends invite, adds video link
loop.remembers: Who gets priority, your focus blocks

ios_blocks.name: EventKit (EKEventStore)
ios_blocks.why: reads free time and writes the final event to the phone's calendars

ios_blocks.name: App Intents calendar schema (AppSchema.CalendarIntent: createEvent, updateEvent)
ios_blocks.why: lets Siri AI hand scheduling requests to the app

ios_blocks.name: UserNotifications
ios_blocks.why: asks rule-clash questions with quick-answer buttons

ios_blocks.name: AuthenticationServices (ASWebAuthenticationSession)
ios_blocks.why: OAuth to Google Calendar or Microsoft Graph for server-side availability

hard_parts: Replies arrive while the phone sleeps, so the agent has to run on a server against Google or Microsoft calendars; on-device EventKit is only a mirror.
Time zones, travel time and soft holds are where these agents embarrass you. One wrong offer costs more than five manual emails.
The other side is more and more often an agent too. Two assistants can loop, double-book or each wait for the other to propose.
Texting is gated: a native iMessage thread for a business agent needs Apple Messages for Business approval (Poke was the first AI agent approved, in June 2026).
risks: Leaking your schedule: offered times, event titles or other attendees reveal more than you meant to share.
Commitments in your name to the wrong person or at the wrong hour, especially across time zones.
assumptions: The other side accepts negotiating with an assistant, and will more and more often be one.
People keep their calendars accurate enough for an agent to trust what looks free.
unknowns: When both sides have agents, who proposes, and what shared protocol will they use?
Will Siri AI's calendar actions turn standalone scheduling assistants into a feature instead of a product?

prior_art.name: Howie
prior_art.note: Scheduling assistant with its own email address and phone number; negotiates over email and iMessage. Reports 1,000+ paying customers.

prior_art.name: Motion
prior_art.note: Auto-scheduling calendar; its iPhone app views and edits while the planning engine runs on desktop.

prior_art.name: Reclaim.ai
prior_art.note: Habit and focus-time blocking; no native iOS app.

prior_art.name: Claude on iOS (Calendar)
prior_art.note: Creates and edits Calendar events on the phone, but does not negotiate with other people.

prior_art.name: Clockwise
prior_art.note: Team calendar optimizer, reportedly shut down in March 2026.

ideas.first_version: An email address you CC. It reads the thread, checks your Google Calendar over the API, offers three times in one reply and sends the invite when the other side picks one. The iPhone app lists open negotiations and asks you only when a request breaks a rule you set.
ideas.notes_for_editor: The Clockwise shutdown and its purchase by Salesforce come from a comparison blog and are unconfirmed. Howie's customer and meeting counts are self-reported. The candidate said Reclaim is owned by Dropbox; I did not re-verify that, so I left it out.

ideas.title: Trip booking and rebooking agents
ideas.tagline: Agents that search and book trips and, when a flight dies, propose a rebooking before you reach the desk.
ideas.moment: Your 6pm connection is cancelled while you are still in the air. When you land, a notification already lists two rebooking options and a hotel hold near the airport. You tap the second one, confirm with Face ID, and walk past the rebooking line.
ideas.problem: Booking a trip is a solved search problem; fixing one that breaks is not. After a cancellation you race hundreds of other passengers through a phone queue, the airline app and the desk. Travel apps tell you the flight is cancelled but rarely hold a seat or a room, and the airline's automatic rebooking picks what suits the airline.

loop.trigger: Flight delay, cancel or schedule change
loop.senses: Flight status, open seats, hotels, rules
loop.decides: Best options for arrival time and cost
loop.checks_with_you: Any change that costs money or moves dates
loop.acts: Rebooks, holds a hotel, updates the trip
loop.remembers: Airlines, seats, connections you prefer

ios_blocks.name: ActivityKit (Live Activities, push-to-start)
ios_blocks.why: a disruption card on the Lock Screen and Watch with options and countdowns

ios_blocks.name: UserNotifications (time-sensitive interruption level)
ios_blocks.why: breaks through Focus when a flight is cancelled

ios_blocks.name: LocalAuthentication
ios_blocks.why: Face ID on any change that costs money

ios_blocks.name: CryptoKit (SecureEnclave)
ios_blocks.why: signs the approval so the server can verify it came from your phone

ios_blocks.name: PassKit (PKPass, PKDeferredPaymentRequest)
ios_blocks.why: updates boarding passes in Wallet and sets up an Apple Pay hotel hold

ios_blocks.name: EventKit
ios_blocks.why: moves flight and hotel events when the plan changes

ios_blocks.name: App Intents (AppEntity, IndexedEntity)
ios_blocks.why: exposes trips and legs to Siri AI, as Tripsy does

hard_parts: Write access. Changing a ticket needs airline or agency access (NDC or a GDS). A plain consumer app can only relay the carrier's offer or deep-link into its app.
Speed. Seats go within minutes of a mass cancellation, so the agent needs status and inventory faster than the airline's own push.

App Review guideline 5.1.1(ix) says apps in regulated fields such as air travel must be submitted by the entity that provides the service, so a booking agent must be, or partner with, a licensed seller.
The airline often rebooks you automatically first, and the agent has to reconcile that before proposing anything.
risks: Two tickets or none, if the agent books a new flight without cleanly releasing the old one.
Under US rules, accepting a rebooking after a cancellation can waive the cash refund the traveller was owed; the agent must show that trade-off.
The agent turns into a messenger for the airline's offer and misses better fixes, such as another airline or a train.
assumptions: Airlines will let a third-party agent change a ticket rather than routing every change through their own app.
Stressed travellers will trust one Face ID tap to spend money on a new plan.
unknowns: Will airlines expose rebooking offers to outside agents through NDC or agent protocols?
Who is liable when the agent's rebooking breaks a connection the airline would have protected?
Will 'self-healing' trips come from booking platforms like Expedia, or from independent agents?

prior_art.name: Expedia + Layla
prior_art.note: Conversational planner and booker bought in July 2026; 'self-healing' trips are planned, not shipped, and tied to Expedia inventory.

prior_art.name: Google AI Mode hotel booking
prior_art.note: Agentic hotel booking in Search since August 2026; booking, not disruption handling.

prior_art.name: Meta Muse travel
prior_art.note: Books flights through the Duffel API inside a general agent; no reported disruption monitoring.

prior_art.name: Hopper HTS Assist
prior_art.note: Cancels, refunds and rebooks through airline systems without a human, but is sold to travel businesses rather than working for the traveller.

ideas.first_version: Watch flights the user forwards by email. On a cancellation or long delay, pull same-day options from a flight data API, rank them by arrival time, and push a Live Activity with two choices and deep links to the airline's own rebooking page. Add a one-tap hotel hold through a booking partner before attempting any ticket changes.
ideas.deep_dive:
## Deep dive

Trip disruption is the clearest case of the pattern most iPhone agents now follow. A server watches and does the work. The phone is where you see the problem and say yes. The window to act is short and a wrong move costs a night in an airport, so every weak spot in the design shows.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Feed as Flight status feed
  participant Agent as Cloud agent
  participant Seller as Booking partner
  participant Phone as iPhone app
  participant You as You
  Feed->>Agent: Your 6pm connection is cancelled
  Agent->>Seller: Search same-day seats and nearby hotels
  Seller-->>Agent: Three flights, two hotels
  Agent->>Agent: Rank by arrival time, cost and your rules
  Agent->>Phone: Push-to-start Live Activity
  Phone->>You: Two options and a hotel hold
  You->>Phone: Pick option 2, confirm with Face ID
  Phone->>Agent: Signed approval
  Agent->>Seller: Book seat and hold room
  Seller-->>Agent: Confirmed, new record locator
  Agent->>Phone: Update Live Activity, Wallet and Calendar
  Phone->>You: New boarding pass and hotel address
```

The phone never hosts the loop. iOS will not keep an app running for hours, so the agent lives on a server that follows flight status. The phone gets a push-to-start Live Activity, which appears even when the app is not running. After Face ID, the app signs the approval with a Secure Enclave key, so the server can prove the yes came from this phone and not from a stolen session.

### What the first 90 days look like

- Weeks 1-4: import trips from forwarded confirmation emails and watch every leg. Measure how many minutes ahead of the airline's own alert you spot a problem.
- Weeks 5-8: on a cancellation or long delay, show ranked options with deep links to the airline's rebooking page, and hold a hotel room through a booking partner. The traveller still makes the ticket change in the airline's app.
- Weeks 9-12: sign an agency partner that can change tickets for one or two carriers, and turn on one-tap rebooking for them. Track how often travellers take the first option, and how often the airline's automatic rebooking was better.

### The hardest engineering problem

Keeping one true version of the trip while three parties change it. The airline often rebooks you on its own within minutes. Your agent is proposing something else. The traveller may be at the desk doing a third thing. The agent has to reconcile all of that before it books, or someone ends up with two tickets or none. That takes idempotent booking calls, holds that expire on a timer, a fresh check of the ticket right before any change, and a log of which record locator is live. The agent also has to know when not to act. Under US rules, accepting a new flight after a cancellation can mean giving up the cash refund the traveller was owed, so "take the refund and book elsewhere" must stay on the menu.

### How it makes money

- Booking commissions and hotel affiliate fees on the rebooked flight and the emergency room.
- A yearly subscription for frequent travellers, priced like a lounge pass.
- Deals with card issuers and travel insurers, which pay out less when stranded travellers are rebooked fast.
ideas.why_flagship: The pattern the whole iPhone agent industry converged on: cloud does the work, the Lock Screen asks for the OK.
ideas.notes_for_editor: That Muse uses Duffel comes from PhocusWire; I did not check it independently. Expedia's 'self-healing' trips wording comes from Expedia and Skift coverage. Hopper HTS Assist details come from VentureBeat. The US refund point describes DOT's general cancellation-refund rule and is not tied to one source in the research notes.

ideas.title: Price-watch auto-buy agents
ideas.tagline: Set a target price once; the agent watches the item and buys when it drops, within a budget you set.
ideas.moment: You want a specific stroller, but not at $480. You tell the shopping agent 'buy it at 30% off, black, ship to home.' Three weeks later a notification says it bought it for $329 and shows the return window.
ideas.problem: Prices on big purchases swing, and the best price can last only hours. Price-alert apps tell you about a drop, but by the time you look the deal may be gone, and you still have to check the seller, the color and the delivery date. A standing order that buys on your terms takes the watching off your plate.

loop.trigger: The price crosses your target
loop.senses: Price, seller, variant, delivery date
loop.decides: Does this offer meet every rule you set?
loop.checks_with_you: One tap, or none if under your cap
loop.acts: Checks out with saved payment and address
loop.remembers: Orders, return windows, price history

ios_blocks.name: Visual Intelligence (IntentValueQuery, SemanticContentDescriptor)
ios_blocks.why: snap a product with the camera to start tracking it

ios_blocks.name: Share extension (NSExtensionContext)
ios_blocks.why: send a product link from Safari or another app to the watch list

ios_blocks.name: PassKit (Apple Pay, PKPaymentAuthorizationController)
ios_blocks.why: user-confirmed checkout; Apple Pay needs a Face ID tap per purchase

ios_blocks.name: UserNotifications
ios_blocks.why: 'price hit' and 'bought it' alerts with approve and cancel actions

ios_blocks.name: WidgetKit
ios_blocks.why: tracked items and their current prices on the Home Screen

ios_blocks.name: App Intents
ios_blocks.why: 'watch this price' from Siri and Shortcuts

hard_parts: Apple has no agent-payment API. True auto-buy on iPhone runs on a store's saved card (Amazon), Google Pay, one-time cards (Stripe Link) or card-network agent tokens, not Apple Pay.
Matching the exact item. Variant, condition, seller rating and delivery date all have to match, or the 'deal' is a different product.
Buying on stores you don't control. Buy for Me-style checkout breaks on login walls, bot checks and redesigns, and merchant protocols such as UCP and ACP cover only some stores.
risks: The agent ranks results for the store, not for you, when the platform that sells is also the one running the agent.
A stale rule fires months later after your needs changed. Rules need expiry dates and a spend cap.
Price-glitch or marketplace-fraud listings that trigger a buy the merchant later cancels, leaving holds on your card.
assumptions: The agent works for you and not for the store whose search results it ranks.
Stores treat agent-placed orders and returns the same as human ones.
unknowns: Will Apple add spend limits or agent mandates to Apple Pay?
Do people with auto-buy rules end up spending more, not less?

prior_art.name: Amazon Alexa for Shopping (Auto Buy, Buy for Me)
prior_art.note: Replaced Rufus in May 2026; buys at your target price and checks out on other sites. Works for Amazon's own catalog first.

prior_art.name: Google agentic checkout and Universal Cart
prior_art.note: Buys through Google Pay at your target price after you confirm; limited to participating merchants.

prior_art.name: ChatGPT Instant Checkout (discontinued)
prior_art.note: In-chat buying dropped in March 2026 after Walmart saw it convert about 3x worse than a click-through to its site.

prior_art.name: Meta Muse checkout
prior_art.note: Pays with one-time Stripe Link cards inside a general agent; no standing price rules reported.

ideas.first_version: A share-sheet 'watch this' for any product link, with a target price, a variant check and an expiry date. When the price hits, send a time-sensitive notification that opens a prefilled Apple Pay sheet, so buying takes one Face ID tap. Offer true auto-buy only at merchants that support an agent checkout protocol.
ideas.notes_for_editor: The 3x conversion figure is Walmart's measurement as reported by Digital Commerce 360. Visa and Mastercard agent-token rollout details come from secondary sources in the research notes.

ideas.title: Money autopilot agents
ideas.tagline: Link your accounts; the agent plans goals and moves money within your limits, then texts you what it did.
ideas.moment: Payday lands on a Friday. Before you check your balance, the agent has paid the card in full, moved $180 to your trip fund and texted: 'Held back $60 because your car insurance renews Tuesday. Undo?'
ideas.problem: Most people know they should pay the card in full, save for the trip and keep a buffer for bills, but doing it every payday takes attention. Budgeting apps draw charts and leave the moves to you. Bank auto-transfers move fixed amounts and ignore what is about to come due.

loop.trigger: Payday lands or a bill comes due
loop.senses: Balances, transactions, upcoming bills
loop.decides: What to pay, save or hold back
loop.checks_with_you: Anything outside your pre-set rules
loop.acts: Moves money between your own accounts
loop.remembers: Goals, bill dates, what you undid

ios_blocks.name: FinanceKit (FinanceStore, BackgroundDeliveryExtension)
ios_blocks.why: reads Apple Card, Apple Cash and Savings data on device and wakes when it changes (iOS 26); needs a managed entitlement

ios_blocks.name: UserNotifications
ios_blocks.why: 'held back $60, undo?' messages with an undo action

ios_blocks.name: App Intents (UndoableIntent)
ios_blocks.why: registers undo for each money move so it can be reversed from the app or Siri

ios_blocks.name: LocalAuthentication
ios_blocks.why: Face ID to change rules or raise caps

ios_blocks.name: WidgetKit
ios_blocks.why: a safe-to-spend number on the Home Screen

hard_parts: Moving money needs a licensed bank or payments partner and account-to-account rails; the app cannot move funds by itself.
Data coverage. FinanceKit covers Apple's own card products and requires Apple's approval; other banks come through aggregators such as Plaid, with gaps and delays.
Timing. Transfers take days and bills post late, so a plan built on today's balance can overdraw tomorrow.
Undo is not really undo. Reversing a transfer means a new transfer, which can also take days.
risks: Safety line: never make a move that could overdraw an account or miss a bill, and never move money to third parties without a fresh approval.
Recommending investments, loans or insurance can become regulated financial advice.
A stolen phone or hijacked account turns the autopilot into a drain; rule changes need Face ID and a cooling-off delay.
assumptions: Regulators keep treating an agent that moves money between your own accounts as a feature, not as financial advice.
Aggregator data stays accurate and timely enough to act on.
unknowns: How much will people let an agent move before they stop trusting the undo button?
Will US open-banking rules (CFPB section 1033) settle in a form that gives agents stable data access?

prior_art.name: Cleo Autopilot
prior_art.note: Plans goals and acts within user-set limits since February 2026; US-focused, mostly moves between the user's own accounts.

prior_art.name: ChatGPT finances
prior_art.note: Plaid-linked dashboard and Q&A across 12,000+ institutions for US Plus and Pro users; explains, does not move money.

prior_art.name: Rocket Money Rowan
prior_art.note: Reportedly texts savings opportunities and takes text instructions; details come from one trade report.

ideas.first_version: Read-only first: connect accounts, forecast the next 30 days of bills, and on each payday propose three moves with amounts that the user approves with one tap. After four weeks of approvals, offer to make the same moves automatically under a cap, with undo.
ideas.notes_for_editor: Rowan's details come from one PYMNTS report and are unconfirmed. Cleo's capabilities come from its own blog and press release. The Menlo 2026 figures (20% of AI users have given an agent a financial account, 36% email) are from the research notes. FinanceKit country availability was not verified.

ideas.title: Bill-fighting and cancel agents
ideas.tagline: An agent calls, emails and chats with companies to lower bills, cancel subscriptions and chase refunds.
ideas.moment: Your internet bill jumped $25 when the promo ended. You forward the bill and tap 'negotiate.' Two days later the agent reports it waited 40 minutes on hold, got a $20-a-month credit, and needs your OK before accepting a 12-month term.
ideas.problem: Companies make cancelling and negotiating slow: long holds, retention menus and 'call during business hours'. People who push get discounts, and most people don't have the time. Services that negotiate for a cut of the savings have existed for years, but they cover a short list of providers.

loop.trigger: You forward a bill or tap 'lower this'
loop.senses: Bill PDF, account details, current offers
loop.decides: Target price, and when to walk away
loop.checks_with_you: Before new contracts, PINs or offers
loop.acts: Calls, emails and chats with the company
loop.remembers: Offers won, promo end dates, follow-ups

ios_blocks.name: Share extension (NSExtensionContext)
ios_blocks.why: forward a bill PDF or screenshot from Mail, Files or Photos

ios_blocks.name: VisionKit (VNDocumentCameraViewController)
ios_blocks.why: scan a paper bill

ios_blocks.name: Vision OCRTool with Foundation Models
ios_blocks.why: reads amounts, dates and the account number on device before anything is uploaded

ios_blocks.name: ActivityKit (Live Activities)
ios_blocks.why: hold and progress status during a long call

ios_blocks.name: UserNotifications
ios_blocks.why: 'accept this offer?' approvals

ios_blocks.name: EventKit
ios_blocks.why: a reminder to recheck before the new promo ends

hard_parts: Account verification. Providers ask for PINs, last-four digits or the account holder, so the agent needs the user pre-authorized on the account or patched into the call.
Retention desks push new contracts, bundles and equipment swaps. The agent has to tell which 'savings' cost more over 12 months.
Follow-through. Credits show up on the next bill or not at all, so the agent must check the next statement and call back.
Calls come from cloud telephony because iOS gives apps no access to cellular calls.
risks: Signing the user up for a contract, early-termination fee or price lock they didn't want.
A third party holding account PINs and ID numbers; a breach makes SIM-swap fraud easier.
Fees based on a share of savings can reward small cuts that come with long contracts.
assumptions: Retention desks keep offering discounts once most of their callers are agents that never give up.
Providers keep accepting an authorized third party acting on the account.
unknowns: After a US court struck down the FTC's click-to-cancel rule in 2025, will state laws make cancelling easy enough that agents aren't needed?
What success rate do these agents reach across providers, beyond self-reported numbers?

prior_art.name: Pine AI
prior_art.note: Calls, emails and web tasks to negotiate bills, cancel and file refunds. Claims $300+ average yearly savings; an independent test saw 2 of 3 tasks succeed in 48 hours.

prior_art.name: Rocket Money Rowan
prior_art.note: Reportedly cancels subscriptions by text instruction; unconfirmed.

prior_art.name: Meta Muse
prior_art.note: Negotiates prices and bills, including through WhatsApp, as one feature of a general agent.

prior_art.name: Cleo Autopilot
prior_art.note: Bill negotiation is on the 2026 roadmap, not shipped.

ideas.first_version: Cancellations only, for the 30 most common subscriptions and a few big US cable and phone providers. The user forwards a bill; the agent cancels through the cheapest channel (web, chat, email, then phone) and reports a confirmation number. Add negotiation once cancelling is reliable.
ideas.notes_for_editor: Pine's 93% success rate and $300+ savings are self-reported; the 2-of-3 test comes from a third-party review listed in the research notes, which I did not open. Rowan is unconfirmed. The FTC click-to-cancel point is from general knowledge (the Eighth Circuit vacated the rule in July 2025), not from the research notes.

ideas.title: Health-record reading assistants
ideas.tagline: Assistants that read Apple Health and medical records to explain labs and prep you for appointments.
ideas.moment: Your yearly bloodwork posts to the patient portal at 9pm. You ask the assistant what changed; it pulls last year's labs and your sleep and activity trends, and drafts three questions for Thursday's appointment.
ideas.problem: Lab results often arrive before the doctor explains them, as a wall of numbers and red flags. Records are split across portals, the Health app and paper. Patient portals show results but don't compare them over time or connect them to how you sleep and move.

loop.trigger: New results, or an appointment is near
loop.senses: Records, labs, meds, sleep, activity
loop.decides: What changed and what is worth asking
loop.checks_with_you: You pick which data types it can read
loop.acts: Explains results, drafts visit questions
loop.remembers: Med list, past results, open questions

ios_blocks.name: HealthKit (HKClinicalRecord)
ios_blocks.why: reads FHIR labs, conditions and medications downloaded from providers; read-only

ios_blocks.name: HealthKit Medications API (HKUserAnnotatedMedication, HKMedicationDoseEvent)
ios_blocks.why: reads the med list and logged doses (iOS 26)

ios_blocks.name: Foundation Models (PrivateCloudComputeLanguageModel)
ios_blocks.why: summarizes on Apple's servers with a 32K context, without sending records to a third-party AI

ios_blocks.name: EventKit
ios_blocks.why: finds the next appointment and attaches the questions

ios_blocks.name: UserNotifications
ios_blocks.why: a prep reminder the evening before a visit

hard_parts: HealthKit rules. Data may go only to services that provide health or fitness services to the user, never to ads or data mining, and App Review 5.1.2(i) requires consent that names any third-party AI.
Coverage. Health Records only work when the user's provider supports the download, and coverage varies by provider and country.
Context size. A few years of FHIR labs plus daily sleep data overflow the 4,096-token on-device model; it needs summarizing or PCC's 32K context.
The Health store is encrypted while the phone is locked, so a background job cannot read new records until the user next opens the phone.
risks: Safety line: explain and compare, never diagnose or suggest changing a medication, and send urgent values straight to a clinician.
Records in a chatbot company's cloud may fall outside HIPAA, which mostly covers providers and insurers, not consumer apps.
Features that interpret results for treatment can become a regulated medical device, and Apple now asks health apps to declare regulated-device status.
assumptions: People trust a chatbot company with their records more than their hospital's own portal.
Providers keep sending records into Apple Health in a usable FHIR format.
unknowns: Will Apple's own Health app summaries, previewed in the iOS 27.2 beta, make third-party readers redundant?
Does reading records change health outcomes, or mostly lower anxiety before visits?

prior_art.name: ChatGPT Health
prior_art.note: Apple Health plus medical records, lab comparisons and visit prep; US rollout began July 23, 2026. Reads and explains, rarely acts.

prior_art.name: Claude Apple Health integration
prior_art.note: Apple Health analysis in beta for US Pro and Max users since January 2026.

prior_art.name: Apple Health AI coach (shelved)
prior_art.note: Apple's own coach (Project Mulberry) was delayed and scaled back, leaving the field to chatbot companies.

ideas.first_version: An on-device lab diff. Read clinical lab records from HealthKit, show what changed since last time with plain-language notes and reference ranges, and add three draft questions to the next appointment in Calendar. Nothing leaves the phone except through Apple's Private Cloud Compute.
ideas.notes_for_editor: The redesigned Health app and Readiness score in the iOS 27.2 beta are reported, not confirmed. The Mulberry shelving comes from press reports. The regulated-device declaration (Health & Fitness and Medical apps, since March 2026) comes from the research notes.

ideas.title: Wearable-driven training coaches
ideas.tagline: Coaches that rewrite today's workout from last night's sleep, HRV and strain, then nudge you on the wrist.
ideas.moment: You slept five hours and your HRV is well below your normal. At 6:30am your coach swaps the interval run for an easy 30 minutes, moves the hard session to Thursday, and tells you why in two lines. The easy run is already on your Watch when you lace up.
ideas.problem: Training plans are written weeks ahead. They don't know you slept badly, caught a cold or had a brutal week at work. Wearables collect the signals but mostly hand you a score and leave the decision to you. The job is turning last night's data into today's session and moving the rest of the week around it, without you rebuilding the plan by hand.

loop.trigger: Morning sync of overnight sleep and HRV
loop.senses: Sleep, HRV, resting HR, recent load
loop.decides: Train hard, go easy, or rest; what to move
loop.checks_with_you: Asks before moving key sessions
loop.acts: Rewrites today's session, syncs it to Watch
loop.remembers: How you felt after past low-HRV days

ios_blocks.name: HealthKit (HKObserverQuery, background delivery)
ios_blocks.why: wakes the app when new sleep, HRV and resting heart rate samples arrive

ios_blocks.name: HealthKit workout zones (HKWorkoutZoneGroup, iOS 27)
ios_blocks.why: reads time in each heart-rate zone to measure real training load

ios_blocks.name: WorkoutKit (WorkoutScheduler)
ios_blocks.why: puts the rewritten interval or easy session on Apple Watch

ios_blocks.name: Foundation Models (SystemLanguageModel, PrivateCloudComputeLanguageModel)
ios_blocks.why: writes the two-line reason and answers questions, on watchOS 27 too

ios_blocks.name: WidgetKit (Smart Stack widget)
ios_blocks.why: shows today's outlook on the wrist and Lock Screen

ios_blocks.name: EventKit
ios_blocks.why: finds a free slot when a hard session moves to another day

hard_parts: Readiness data is noisy. HRV moves with alcohol, a late meal, illness or a loose band, so the coach needs weeks of your own baseline and must take 'I feel fine' seriously.
HealthKit encrypts its store while the phone is locked, and background delivery for some data types is capped at hourly. The 6:30am decision has to cope with data that arrives late or not at all.
Hardware-neutral is harder than it sounds. Oura, WHOOP, Garmin and Apple Watch each write different subsets of their data to Apple Health, with different delays and sleep staging.
The plan needs real coaching rules underneath (build, taper, coming back from injury). A language model that improvises the plan week to week will drift.
risks: Safety line: it is a training coach, not a doctor. Chest pain, fainting or a resting heart rate far above normal must stop the plan and point to medical care, never just an easier workout.
Health data rules: App Review 5.1.3 bars using HealthKit data for ads and storing personal health data in iCloud, and 5.1.2(i) requires explicit consent before sending it to a third-party model.
People may hand their judgment to a score: skipping sessions they could do, or pushing through pain because the number looks good.
assumptions: That a readiness score reflects how you actually feel well enough to justify changing your plan.
That people wear the device to bed every night, so the morning decision has data.
That a two-line explanation is enough for people to trust a skipped workout.
unknowns: Does adjusting daily training from HRV actually improve results for recreational athletes, or does it just feel smarter?
If Apple ships the Readiness score and coaching it is testing for the Health app, is there room left for a third-party coach?
Can a hardware-neutral coach make money when Google, Oura and WHOOP bundle a coach with the device subscription?

prior_art.name: Google Health / Fitbit Gemini coach
prior_art.note: Builds training plans that adapt to sleep, heart rate and readiness. Reached iOS in February 2026; the Fitbit app became Google Health in May 2026.

prior_art.name: Oura Advisor
prior_art.note: Sleep- and readiness-focused coach with memories of your patterns. Needs the ring.

prior_art.name: WHOOP Coach
prior_art.note: Recovery- and strain-based coaching tied to the WHOOP strap and membership.

prior_art.name: Apple's delayed Health coach
prior_art.note: Apple's own AI coach (Mulberry) was delayed and reportedly scaled back, leaving Watch owners without a first-party coach.

ideas.first_version: An iPhone and Watch app that reads HealthKit each morning and compares HRV and sleep to your own 30-day baseline. It picks one of three versions of today's planned session (as written, easier, rest), sends it to the Watch with WorkoutKit, and explains the choice in two lines. You can override with one tap, and it asks how you felt afterwards.
ideas.notes_for_editor: Apple's scaled-back coach and the Readiness score in the iOS 27.2 beta come from press reports (9to5Mac), not Apple. The candidate's WHOOP quote ('someone to tell me what to do') was not independently verified, so it is left out of the card.

ideas.title: Meeting and memory capture
ideas.tagline: Your phone, Watch or a pendant records the conversation; the agent writes notes, to-dos and follow-ups.
ideas.moment: You walk out of a hallway meeting with a supplier. You tapped record on your Watch when it started, and by the elevator the notes sit under the calendar event with three action items and a drafted follow-up email. You fix one date and send it.
ideas.problem: Notes from in-person meetings, site visits and phone calls get lost or never written. Meeting bots only join video calls, so the hallway, the job site and the doctor's office go uncaptured. The job isn't a transcript. It's the decisions, the to-dos and the follow-up email that should exist ten minutes after the meeting ends.

loop.trigger: You tap record on phone, Watch or pendant
loop.senses: Audio, calendar event, attendee names
loop.decides: Who said what; decisions, to-dos, owners
loop.checks_with_you: Before any follow-up or task is sent
loop.acts: Writes notes, drafts email, files tasks
loop.remembers: Searchable history of past conversations

ios_blocks.name: App Intents (AudioRecordingIntent)
ios_blocks.why: starts capture from the Action button or Control Center with the system recording indicator

ios_blocks.name: ActivityKit (Live Activities)
ios_blocks.why: required while an AudioRecordingIntent records; shows elapsed time on the Lock Screen

ios_blocks.name: AVFAudio (AVAudioSession)
ios_blocks.why: keeps recording after the screen locks

ios_blocks.name: Speech (SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber)
ios_blocks.why: on-device transcription, iOS 26 and later

ios_blocks.name: BackgroundTasks (BGContinuedProcessingTask)
ios_blocks.why: finishes processing a long recording after you leave the app

ios_blocks.name: Foundation Models (@Generable)
ios_blocks.why: pulls decisions, to-dos and owners into structured fields

ios_blocks.name: EventKit
ios_blocks.why: files notes under the matching calendar event and its attendees

ios_blocks.name: WatchConnectivity
ios_blocks.why: moves Watch recordings to the phone

hard_parts: Consent: many US states and countries require everyone's permission to record, and App Review 2.5.14 requires consent plus a visible or audible indicator. An all-day pendant runs straight into this.
Telling speakers apart in a noisy hallway, or when people talk over each other, still fails often. A to-do given to the wrong person is worse than none.
An hour of transcript is too long for the on-device model's context, so summaries need chunking or a server model. A third-party model also needs explicit consent under App Review 5.1.2(i).
Acting on the notes means OAuth into each task tool and email account plus a reliable review step. That is why most products stop at suggested to-dos.
risks: Recording people who didn't agree, especially with always-on pendants. It needs a clear indicator and a one-tap 'off the record'.
A searchable archive of every conversation is a target for breaches, subpoenas and workplace disputes.
Vendor churn: Meta stopped selling Limitless after buying it, so users need a real export or they can lose their archive.
assumptions: That everyone else in the room is fine with being recorded.
That people review and send the drafted follow-ups instead of letting them pile up.
That transcripts get names, numbers and dates right, which is where errors hurt most.
unknowns: Does a lifetime conversation memory get used after the first month, or is the value only in same-day follow-ups?
How will courts and employers treat AI meeting summaries as records?
Will Apple grow its own recording and summary features into follow-up actions and squeeze the independents?

prior_art.name: Granola
prior_art.note: Bot-free meeting notes. The iPhone app captures in-person meetings and links notes to calendar events; one-tap Apple Watch capture since July 2026.

prior_art.name: Plaud NotePin S
prior_art.note: Clip-on recorder (January 2026) with an iPhone app and desktop capture; Plaud reports more than 2.5M users.

prior_art.name: Amazon Bee
prior_art.note: Pendant or wristband that records all day, extracts to-dos and builds a searchable memory; free to use since Amazon bought it.

prior_art.name: Otter Meeting Agent
prior_art.note: Otter's agent pitched as a teammate inside meetings, not only a transcriber.

prior_art.name: Limitless (discontinued)
prior_art.note: Memory pendant whose sales stopped after Meta bought the company in December 2025; shows the archive risk.

ideas.first_version: An iPhone and Watch app that starts recording from the Action button, transcribes on device, and files notes under the matching calendar event. It pulls out decisions and to-dos with owners, and drafts one follow-up email that you edit and send from your own mail app.
ideas.notes_for_editor: Plaud user counts, Bee pricing and the Granola Watch launch date come from company pages and press summarized in the research digest. Otter Meeting Agent's feature set is described only from the blog title.

ideas.title: Family logistics agents
ideas.tagline: A household agent that turns school emails, flyers and texts into shared calendars, chores and grocery orders.
ideas.moment: The school sends a PDF about picture day, a field-trip form and a bake sale. You forward it to the family agent. It puts the dates on both parents' calendars, assigns the form to your partner, adds eggs to the grocery order, and asks you one thing: 'The flyer says the bake sale is Friday the 14th and Thursday the 13th. Which is it?'
ideas.problem: Family plans arrive as school emails, PDFs, group texts and paper flyers, and one parent usually carries the job of turning them into a schedule. Calendar and list apps store plans but don't read the mess. Chatbots can read it but make small date errors, and one missed pickup costs more trust than months of saved minutes.

loop.trigger: You forward an email, text or flyer photo
loop.senses: Dates, deadlines, asks, who is involved
loop.decides: What goes where, who owns it, what's unclear
loop.checks_with_you: Unclear dates and anything that costs money
loop.acts: Adds events, assigns tasks, fills the cart
loop.remembers: Kids' schedules, school quirks, past errors

ios_blocks.name: Share extension (NSExtensionContext)
ios_blocks.why: takes a forwarded email, PDF or screenshot from any app

ios_blocks.name: VisionKit (VNDocumentCameraViewController)
ios_blocks.why: scans paper flyers and permission slips

ios_blocks.name: Foundation Models (@Generable)
ios_blocks.why: extracts dates, places and asks on device, keeping the source sentence

ios_blocks.name: EventKit
ios_blocks.why: writes events to a shared family calendar and tasks to Reminders

ios_blocks.name: CloudKit (CKShare)
ios_blocks.why: shares the household's task list and status between parents

ios_blocks.name: User Notifications (UNNotificationAction)
ios_blocks.why: asks a clarifying question with tap-to-answer buttons

ios_blocks.name: App Intents
ios_blocks.why: answers 'What's on tomorrow?' from Siri or Shortcuts

hard_parts: Extraction accuracy is the product. School emails say 'next Friday', repeat last year's dates and send corrections in a later thread. Milo shut down in January 2026 because small errors made scheduling more work, not less.
iOS apps can't read your Mail or Messages, so everything has to be forwarded, shared or photographed, or pulled through Gmail or Outlook OAuth that a parent must set up.
Split custody, grandparents and carpools mean the agent must know whose week it is and must not leak one household's details to the other.
Grocery ordering depends on partner integrations (Ohai uses Instacart), and substitutions still need a person.
risks: A wrong pickup time or a missed permission slip lands on a child. Every date the agent is unsure about must be shown with its source, not guessed.
School messages hold minors' names, health notes and locations. Keep extraction on device where possible and get explicit consent before sending anything to a third-party model (App Review 5.1.2(i)).
It can quietly shift the mental load onto whichever parent gets the approval pings.
assumptions: That one wrong date costs less trust than the agent saves in time. Milo found the opposite.
That parents will forward things consistently instead of handling them on the spot.
That both parents accept one shared system.
unknowns: What error rate will parents tolerate before they stop trusting the calendar?
Will schools and their messaging vendors ever publish structured event feeds, making extraction unnecessary?
Can a family agent charge $10 a month when Apple, Google and Amazon bundle household assistants?

prior_art.name: Ohai 'O'
prior_art.note: Household manager through an app and SMS: shared lists, tasks, meal plans and Instacart orders for $9.99/month. Mostly lists and groceries so far.

prior_art.name: Milo (shut down)
prior_art.note: SMS family assistant backed by OpenAI and YC; closed in January 2026 after its founder said AI was too early to be reliable for family scheduling.

prior_art.name: Poke
prior_art.note: General iMessage agent with calendar and email access; not built around family roles or co-parent coordination.

ideas.first_version: A share extension and forwarding address that turns one school email, PDF or flyer photo into proposed calendar events and tasks, each showing the sentence it came from. Nothing lands on the family calendar until a parent taps confirm, and anything ambiguous comes back as a question.
ideas.notes_for_editor: Ohai's price and founder (Care.com's Sheila Lirio Marcelo) and Milo's shutdown reasons come from the research digest, tagged likely rather than verified.

ideas.title: Messaging-native personal agents
ideas.tagline: A personal agent you text in iMessage or WhatsApp; it watches your accounts and texts you first.
ideas.moment: At 6:10am a text arrives from your agent: 'Your 9am moved to 9:30 and check-in for your flight is open. Check you in and tell Sam you'll be late?' You reply 'yes both' and put the phone down. A minute later: 'Done. Boarding pass is in your email, and Sam has your note.'
ideas.problem: People check their messages hundreds of times a day but open a new app only when they remember to. Most assistants wait to be asked, live in their own app and can't reach the accounts where the work is. The job is an agent that watches mail and calendar, notices what needs doing, and asks in the thread you already read.

loop.trigger: New mail, calendar change, or your text
loop.senses: Gmail, Calendar, Slack, Notion via OAuth
loop.decides: What needs you now and what it can handle
loop.checks_with_you: Yes/no reply in the thread before acting
loop.acts: Runs the steps server-side, replies done
loop.remembers: Your preferences, contacts, past answers

ios_blocks.name: Apple Messages for Business
ios_blocks.why: Apple's registered business-chat channel, so the agent can be the other side of an iMessage thread (a service, not an SDK)

ios_blocks.name: AuthenticationServices (ASWebAuthenticationSession)
ios_blocks.why: connects Gmail, Outlook, Slack and Notion with OAuth in the companion app

ios_blocks.name: App Intents (messages schema: sendMessage, draftMessage)
ios_blocks.why: lets Siri AI hand a request to the agent's companion app

ios_blocks.name: Suggested Actions (SuggestedActionsView, iOS 27)
ios_blocks.why: offers Calendar and Reminders actions under the agent's messages in its own app

ios_blocks.name: User Notifications
ios_blocks.why: fallback alerts for users who don't use a messaging channel

hard_parts: iOS apps can't read your iMessages, so the agent has to be the other side of the conversation: Messages for Business, its own phone number or WhatsApp. Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on Messages for Business only in June 2026.

Prompt injection: the agent reads mail and invites written by strangers and then acts. A crafted invite can tell it to forward files, so it must treat that content as data only and confirm anything that sends, shares or pays.
A text thread is a weak approval screen. 'Yes' to a two-part question is ambiguous, and there is no Face ID step in a chat bubble.
Watching many accounts means server-side webhooks or polling and a model call per event, which costs money before the user sees any value.
risks: A spoofed or hijacked thread becomes a remote control for your email and calendar. Forwarded or quoted text must never count as approval.
An agent that texts first can turn into the notification noise it was meant to cut.
Platform dependence: Apple or Meta can change what automated business messaging may do.
assumptions: That Apple keeps Messages for Business open to general-purpose agents, not just airlines and banks.
That people will give one startup OAuth access to their email, calendar and work tools.
That short yes/no replies give the agent enough context to act correctly.
unknowns: How do you add a strong approval step (Face ID, a spend limit) to a chat-only agent without sending people to an app?
Will Siri AI's cross-app actions make a separate texting agent unnecessary for iPhone owners?
Who is liable when an agent acts on a 'yes' that was meant for a different question?

prior_art.name: Poke (The Interaction Company)
prior_art.note: Proactive agent used entirely by text. Watches Gmail, Calendar, Outlook, Notion, Slack and GitHub; first AI agent approved on Messages for Business (June 2026).

prior_art.name: Meta Muse in WhatsApp
prior_art.note: Meta's personal agent, usable inside WhatsApp, that shops, writes email and negotiates.

prior_art.name: OpenClaw
prior_art.note: Open-source, self-hosted agent reachable from iMessage, WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal and other channels. Setup needs Terminal skills.

prior_art.name: Howie
prior_art.note: Scheduling assistant with its own email address and number; works over email and iMessage, but only for scheduling.

ideas.first_version: One narrow job done in a text thread: watch Gmail and Google Calendar, text you when a meeting moves or a check-in opens, and make the fix only after you reply yes. Start on its own phone number or WhatsApp while applying for Messages for Business.
ideas.notes_for_editor: Poke's 'about 100M messages relayed' is a company claim reported by TechCrunch and is left out of the card. Suggested Actions (iOS 27) works in a messaging app's own chat view, not in Apple's Messages app. Messages for Business has no public iOS framework in current docs; it is listed as a service.

ideas.title: Self-hosted agents, iPhone as node
ideas.tagline: Run your own agent on a home server; the iPhone app lends it the camera, location and your approvals.
ideas.moment: Your agent runs on a Mac mini at home. In the store it pings you through the iPhone app: 'Snap the shelf so I can check prices against your list?' You open the app, approve, and take the photo. A minute later it replies in Telegram with what to buy here and what's cheaper online.
ideas.problem: Some people want a capable agent without handing their email and files to a startup, so they run one on their own machine. But a home server can't see where you are, take a photo or ask you a quick question on the go. The phone has to act as the agent's eyes, location and approval button without becoming a hole into your home network.

loop.trigger: Remote agent requests a phone capability
loop.senses: Camera, location, calendar, contacts
loop.decides: Gateway plans; phone enforces allowlist
loop.checks_with_you: Approval prompt for each sensitive command
loop.acts: Snaps photo, shares location, adds reminder
loop.remembers: Pairing keys and per-command permissions

ios_blocks.name: Foundation (URLSessionWebSocketTask)
ios_blocks.why: holds the link to the self-hosted gateway while the app is open

ios_blocks.name: User Notifications (UNNotificationAction)
ios_blocks.why: approve or deny a gateway request from the Lock Screen

ios_blocks.name: AVFoundation (AVCapturePhotoOutput)
ios_blocks.why: takes the photo the agent asked for, in the foreground only

ios_blocks.name: Core Location (CLMonitor, significant-change service)
ios_blocks.why: geofence and presence events that still run in the background

ios_blocks.name: EventKit, Contacts, PhotoKit
ios_blocks.why: calendar, reminder, contact and photo commands, each behind its own iOS permission

ios_blocks.name: LocalAuthentication
ios_blocks.why: Face ID before high-risk commands such as sharing contacts

hard_parts: iOS suspends the app and its socket in the background. OpenClaw documents camera, screen and talk commands as blocked there; only location events and presence keep working. Most requests need a push that brings you back into the app.
Reaching a home machine from a cellular connection needs a tunnel or VPN, on top of a setup that already needs Terminal skills.

Memory poisoning is a live threat: the GhostWriter study (2026) got hidden payloads into personal agents' long-term memory about 98% of the time. A phone node adds camera and location to whatever an attacker can steer.
Approval prompts have to say exactly what and why ('photo of the shelf, for the grocery task'), or people approve blindly.
risks: A hijacked gateway can ask the phone for photos, location or contacts. Per-command approval, short-lived grants and a visible log are the main defenses.
Approval fatigue: after fifty prompts a day, people stop reading them.
No company stands behind the security; fixes depend on volunteers and on each user updating.
assumptions: That people who self-host an agent also secure it, now that a phone node makes it more powerful.
That App Review keeps approving a thin client that takes orders from an agent Apple never reviews.
That users keep a home machine running all the time.
unknowns: Can a zero-setup version exist (a hosted gateway with the same privacy) without becoming just another cloud agent?
Will Apple ever let a paired agent call App Intents on the phone, the way Siri can?
How should approvals scale when an agent needs the phone dozens of times a day?

ideas.title: On-phone app builders
ideas.tagline: Describe an app on your iPhone; an agent writes it, builds it on cloud Macs and sends it to TestFlight.
ideas.moment: On the train you describe a tip-splitting app for your climbing group. The agent writes SwiftUI, builds it on a cloud Mac, and 20 minutes later a TestFlight invite arrives. You try it, say 'make the buttons bigger', and a new build lands before your stop.
ideas.problem: People with an idea for a small app can't write Swift, and a Mac with Xcode is a big first step. Chat tools can write code but can't compile, sign or ship it. The job is going from a sentence to an app on your own phone, and later to the App Store, with building, signing and review steps handled for you.

hard_parts: App Review 2.5.2 bans apps that download or run code that changes features. Apple blocked updates for Replit and Vibecode and pulled Anything in March 2026. The builders that survived moved previews to an external browser and compiling to cloud Macs.
App Review 4.2.6 rejects apps made by an app-generation service unless the content owner submits them, so each app has to ship under the user's own developer account.
macOS builds must run on Apple hardware, so every build minute costs real Mac time and fleets are slow to scale.
Generated apps break in quiet ways (state bugs, missing privacy strings, crashes on older phones) that a non-coder can't diagnose.
risks: A flood of near-identical apps that App Review rejects as spam (4.3), wasting users' time and money.
Generated apps that touch health, money or kids' data can ship without the privacy handling the rules require, and the user, not the builder, is the developer of record.
One App Review interpretation can freeze the product, as March 2026 showed.
assumptions: That Apple keeps tolerating builders as long as the generated code runs anywhere except inside the reviewed app.
That non-developers will pay Apple's $99 yearly developer fee to ship their app.
That most people want a personal tool on their own phone more than an App Store listing.
unknowns: Will Apple ever offer a sanctioned path for personal, unreviewed apps beyond TestFlight?
Can generated apps be kept working a year later when iOS changes, or do they rot?
Does agentic coding inside Xcode 27 turn phone-first builders into a niche?

ideas.title: CarPlay voice agents
ideas.tagline: Talk to an AI assistant through CarPlay; it answers, drafts and plans, then hands follow-ups to your phone.
ideas.moment: You are 40 minutes from home and remember the dentist form due tomorrow. You tap the assistant on the car screen and ask it to draft the email to the office and remind you to print the form when you get home. The draft is waiting in the app when you park.
ideas.problem: Drive time is long, hands-busy and full of things you remember but can't act on. Siri handles short commands, and until 2026 other assistants weren't allowed on the car screen. The job is a spoken conversation that turns 'I need to deal with X' into drafts, plans and reminders waiting on your phone when you stop.

loop.trigger: You tap the assistant on the car screen
loop.senses: Your voice, location, calendar
loop.decides: Answer now, or queue a task for later
loop.checks_with_you: Drafts wait on the phone until you park
loop.acts: Answers aloud, drafts, saves follow-ups
loop.remembers: Open tasks and trips you've asked about

ios_blocks.why: two-way audio that ducks music and handles call interruptions

hard_parts: Apple's limits: voice only, no wake word, and no control of the car or iPhone functions. The app can't send a message itself; it has to queue the task for later.
Answers must be short and interruptible, and anything that needs reading or tapping has to wait until you're parked.
Tunnels and rural roads drop the cloud model mid-sentence, so it needs a graceful 'I'll finish this when you're back online'.
ChatGPT, Perplexity, Grok and Meta AI already ship general assistants in CarPlay, so a newcomer needs a specific job: an EV road-trip planner, a field-service log or a trip concierge.
risks: Driver distraction: long or emotional conversations pull attention off the road even when they're eyes-free.
Confident wrong answers about roads, closures or local laws at speed.
The mic hears everyone in the car, so it needs a clear indicator and no silent keeping of passengers' speech (App Review 2.5.14).
assumptions: That drivers want a general chatbot more than an agent that knows this particular trip.
That in-car conversations stay short enough to be safe.
That Apple keeps widening what CarPlay voice apps may do instead of reserving actions for Siri.
unknowns: Will Apple allow a wake word or steering-wheel button for third-party assistants?
Do drivers use these assistants every week, or was it a launch novelty?
How will regulators treat in-car AI conversations under distracted-driving rules?

ideas.title: AI conversation tutors
ideas.tagline: Speak with an AI character that adapts mid-conversation; strong at talk, weak at planning your practice week.
ideas.moment: Before your trip to Madrid you do a ten-minute video call with an AI tutor. She notices you avoid the past tense, steers the chat to your weekend, and corrects you gently without stopping the flow. It feels like practice with a patient friend.
ideas.problem: Speaking is the hardest skill to practice alone, and human tutors cost money and need scheduling. AI tutors now hold a real conversation and adapt within it. But they stop when the call ends: they don't plan your week, tie practice to your trip date, or push you toward real conversations with people.

loop.trigger: You start a session or a reminder fires
loop.senses: Your speech, errors, pace, past sessions
loop.decides: Topic, difficulty, which errors to fix now
loop.checks_with_you: Nothing: acts within the lesson
loop.acts: Talks, corrects, role-plays, sets a drill
loop.remembers: Weak spots, vocabulary, goals and dates

ios_blocks.name: AVFAudio (AVAudioEngine, AVAudioSession)
ios_blocks.why: low-latency two-way voice

ios_blocks.name: Speech (SpeechTranscriber)
ios_blocks.why: on-device transcripts to mark errors after a session

ios_blocks.why: shows a quick translation when you get stuck

ios_blocks.why: turns a session transcript into a structured list of errors to drill

ios_blocks.name: EventKit
ios_blocks.why: books short practice sessions before a trip or exam date

ios_blocks.name: User Notifications
ios_blocks.why: reminds you of the next session

hard_parts: Latency: a pause of more than a beat breaks the feel of conversation, so most tutors stream audio to cloud speech models, which costs money every minute.
Correcting without killing flow: too many corrections stop learners talking; too few let errors set in.
Speech recognition does worse on learners' accented, halting speech, which makes pronunciation feedback hard to trust.
The agentic step (planning the week, tying practice to a date, setting up real conversations with people) needs calendar access and matching with other people, and none of the leaders has built it.
risks: Children use these apps. Voice recordings of minors need short retention and parental consent.
False fluency: learners do well with a patient AI and then freeze with fast, impatient native speakers.
Streaks and engagement numbers can replace real progress as the thing the product optimizes.
assumptions: That fluency comes from more minutes of AI conversation rather than from being pushed into real conversations with people.
That learners are willing to speak aloud to a phone at home or in public.
That per-minute voice model costs keep falling fast enough for cheap tiers.
unknowns: Do AI conversation minutes carry over to real conversations, and how would anyone measure it?
What would an agentic tutor that arranges real-world practice look like without the safety problems of meeting strangers?
Will on-device speech models get good enough to cut the per-minute cloud cost?

ideas.title: Scam-call guardian agents
ideas.tagline: An AI screens unknown callers, flags scam scripts and cloned voices, and alerts family before money moves.
ideas.moment: Your mother gets a call from 'her grandson', crying, who needs bail money today. Because unknown calls route through the guardian's screening line, the agent hears the claim and the payment demand before she does. It pings you: 'Did you just call Mom?' You tap No, and her screen says in large type: 'Blocked a likely scam. Jake is safe.'
ideas.problem: Scam calls now use scripts tuned for panic and, more and more, cloned voices of relatives. Carrier labels and blocklist apps catch known robocall numbers but not a fresh number with a convincing story. Older adults are targeted most, and the family usually hears about the call after the money is gone. The job is to catch the script, not just the number, and pull in someone who can confirm the story fast.

loop.trigger: Unknown or suspicious call comes in
loop.senses: Caller's words, number reputation, voice
loop.decides: Scam script? Claimed relative? Pay demand?
loop.checks_with_you: Named relative confirms; elder can override
loop.acts: Screens, warns, blocks, alerts family
loop.remembers: Trusted callers, blocked numbers, scripts

ios_blocks.why: real-time caller labels from your server through private information retrieval; needs Apple's approval

ios_blocks.why: delivers screened calls as VoIP calls so the audio stays on the screening line

ios_blocks.why: sends 'Did you just call Mom?' to the relative's phone

ios_blocks.why: shows the relative that a flagged call is in progress

ios_blocks.name: App Intents
ios_blocks.why: one press of the Action button asks 'Is this a scam?' during any call

hard_parts: No call audio: iOS gives third-party apps no access to live cellular calls. The agent has to sit in the network (carrier forwarding to a cloud line, or its own VoIP line), which older adults must set up and keep turned on.

Accuracy on real calls: PreScam (2026) found LLMs track scam escalation only moderately well, and TeleAntiFraud 2.0 saw classifiers drop to 0.65-0.68 macro-F1 against similar legitimate calls. Blocking a real doctor's office once can end trust.
Spoofed known numbers: a scammer showing a relative's real number skips unknown-caller routing, so the design also needs a check the elder can start herself.

Apple's free Call Screening (iOS 26) already answers unknown callers and asks their purpose, and Truecaller and RoboKiller already block numbers. A paid guardian has to add what they don't: family in the loop and the whole conversation watched.
risks: Safety line: it must never block emergency services, hospitals or allowlisted contacts, and it must not decide for the elder. It warns and asks, and she can always take the call.
Routing calls through a cloud line means processing the other party's speech, which runs into two-party consent laws. The greeting has to disclose it.
Dignity: an app set up by adult children can slide into monitoring a parent. The elder should see and control every alert rule, and call data must not be reused (App Review 2.5.12).
assumptions: That older adults keep call forwarding and permissions turned on even after the app blocks a real doctor's office once.
That a relative answers a verification ping within a minute or two, day or night.
That carriers keep allowing conditional forwarding to third-party lines.
unknowns: Can voice-clone detection over a phone-quality line stay ahead of cloning tools, or is it a losing race?
Will Apple open call audio or Call Screening results to trusted guardian apps, the way it opened call translation to VoIP apps?
Who is liable when the guardian lets a scam through, or blocks a real emergency call?

If a caller claims to be a relative or asks for money, the named relative gets a Time Sensitive 'Did you just call?' push and the elder gets a plain-language warning. No automatic blocking in the first release.
